4: We divide the corpusD into 100-word passages
5: following previous works on open-domain question
6: answering (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Petroni et al.,
7: 2021; Piktus et al., 2021), in contrast to commer-
8: cial systems like Bing Chat, which cite entire Web
9: pages. We take 100-word passages because it is
10: easier for humans to verify, and allows for more
11: retrieved passages to fit in LLMs’ limited context.
12: We choose QA datasets so that (1) they contain
13: factual questions, in which references are impor-
14: tant; (2) questions require long-text answers that
15: cover multiple aspects; (3) answering the questions
16: requires synthesizing multiple sources. We select
17: three datasets (Table 1) and introduce them below.
18: See §B for additional statistics.
19: ASQA (Stelmakh et al., 2022) is a long-form fac-
20: toid dataset. As shown in Figure 1, each question is
21: an ambiguous question from AmbigQA (Min et al.,
22: 2020) that requires multiple short answers to cover
23: different aspects, and the dataset provides a long-
24: form answer that covers all short answers. Since
25: most questions can be answered by Wikipedia, we
26: use the 2018-12-20 Wikipedia snapshot asD.
27: QAMPARI (Rubin et al., 2022) is a factoid QA
28: dataset constructed from Wikipedia, where the an-
29: swer is a list of entities that are drawn from differ-
30: ent passages. Same as ASQA, we use the 2018-12-
31: 20 Wikipedia as the corpus.
32: ELI5 (Fan et al., 2019) is a long-form QA
33: dataset built on the Reddit forum “Explain Like I’m
34: Five”.6 Most ELI5 questions are how/why/what
35: questions that require long answers and multiple
36: passages as evidence. Due to the diverse topics dis-
37: cussed in the questions, we use Sphere (Piktus et al.,
38: 2021)—a filtered version of Common Crawl 7—as
39: the corpus. The ELI5 dataset is widely used in
40: related work due to its challenging nature (Nakano
41: et al., 2021; Menick et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023).
42: We randomly select 1,000 examples from the
43: development set of each dataset for ALCE. Our
44: benchmark primarily assesses the citation capabili-
45: ties of existing LLMs and does not provide training
46: data, as there are no available examples that pro-
47: vide supervision for citations in these datasets.
48: 6https://www.reddit.com/r/explainlikeimfive/

51: 3 Automatic Evaluation
52: Our benchmark measures the following three di-
53: mensions of system responses:
54: • Fluency: whether the model’s generated text is
55: fluent and coherent.
56: • Correctness: whether the answer is accurate
57: and covers all aspects of interest.
58: • Citation quality: whether the answer is well
59: supported by the cited passages and no irrelevant
60: passages are cited.
61: In the following, we present automatic metrics for
62: each dimension and discuss why the combination
63: of the three metrics provides a robust evaluation.
64: 3.1 Fluency
65: We use MAUVE (Pillutla et al., 2021) to evaluate
66: the fluency of the output (§C). We deploy MAUVE
67: for ASQA and ELI5 and omit it for QAMPARI, as
68: QAMPARI only requires a list of short answers as
69: the response and LLMs consistently adhere to the
70: format in our experiments. As MAUVE is sensitive
71: to output length and text style, and most LLMs are
72: capable of producing fluent text, we mainly employ
73: it as a sanity check as long as the MAUVE scores
74: are high enough.
75: 3.2 Correctness
76: Our objective is to measure the informativeness and
77: utility of the generation to the question. Liu et al.
78: (2023) propose to directly evaluateperceived utility
79: by humans, a process difficult to automate. There-
80: fore, we use correctness—whether the response is
81: accurate compared to a ground truth answer—as a
82: proxy. Evaluating the correctness of long-form gen-
83: eration is a challenging task (Krishna et al., 2021),
84: and we describe our strategy for each dataset be-
85: low. Figure 2 illustrates the metrics and we include
86: additional implementation details in §C.
87: For ASQA, we follow Stelmakh et al. (2022)
88: and calculate the recall of correct short answers by
89: checking whether the short answers (provided by
90: the dataset) are exact substrings of the generation
91: (exact match recall; EM recall).
92: For QAMPARI, we follow Rubin et al. (2022)
93: and calculate the precision and recall of the model
94: prediction, by checking the exact match to the gold
95: answer list. We add one additional adjustment:
96: considering that users often want to know only a
97: few example answers of the question, our evalua-
98: tion considers recall to be 100% if the prediction
99: includes at least 5 correct answers (recall-5).

37: Unlike ASQA and QAMPARI, the ELI5 dataset
38: does not provide short entity answers. Fan et al.
39: (2019) use ROUGE for evaluation, which does
40: not reflect the correctness well (Krishna et al.,
41: 2021; §A). Inspired by works in summariza-
42: tion evaluation (Zhang and Bansal, 2021; Kamoi
43: et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2020), we use Instruct-
44: GPT (text-davinci-003; Ouyang et al., 2022)
45: to generate three “sub-claims”. Then we use
46: TRUE8 (Honovich et al., 2022), a T5-11B (Raf-
47: fel et al., 2020) model fine-tuned on a collection of
48: natural language inference (NLI) datasets, to check
49: whether the model output entails the sub-claims
50: (claim recall). TRUE targets factual correctness
51: and has been used by previous works in similar
52: context (Bohnet et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2023). We
53: demonstrate that claim recall provides a more ac-
54: curate measure of correctness than existing metrics
55: (more details in §A).
56: 3.3 Citation Quality
57: We evaluate citation qualities using two metrics: (1)
58: citation recall, which determines if the output is en-
59: tirely supported by cited passages, and (2) citation
60: precision, which identifies any irrelevant citations.
61: Although we prioritize citation recall as it entails
62: a well-supported and truthful answer, enhancing
63: precision is crucial for better user satisfaction, re-
64: ducing the need for human review of extraneous

1: A Generating Claims for ELI5
2: We elect not to use ROUGE-L as our main cor-
3: rectness metrics since it does not account for the
4: different ways of expressing the same answer and it
5: can be easily gamed (Krishna et al., 2021). We fur-
6: ther illustrate this issue in Table 10. A system can
7: easily achieve high ROUGE-L score by retrieving
8: and returning the top passage from a BM25 index.
9: However, the claims evaluation metric does not
10: reward this approach since the output often lacks
11: different aspects of the answers.

19: Instead, we leverage the original answers to gen-
20: erate sub-claims and use them to serve as an esti-
21: mate of the different aspects of the answers that
22: we expect the model to cover. This approach is
23: inspired by works in summarization evaluation and
24: claim verification (Zhang and Bansal, 2021; Kamoi
25: et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2020).
26: Specifically, we usetext-davinci-003 to gen-
27: erate the sub-claims. We first manually annotate
28: three question and answer pairs from the original
29: ELI5 training set with 3 sub-claims each. Then,
30: we prompt text-davinci-003 with these pairs as
31: demonstrations. The full prompt with an example
32: is shown in Table 22.
33: InstructGPT generates coherent and faithful
34: sub-claims. To ensure that the generated sub-
35: claims are of good quality, we manually inspect
36: a random sample of 40 answers and their generated
37: sub-claims (totaling to 120 sub-claims). For each
38: sub-claim, we assign a score of 1 if it is relevant to
39: the question and faithful to the facts presented in
40: the ground truth, and 0 otherwise. We found that
41: 112 out of the 120 (93.33%) sub-claims received a
42: score of 1, meaning that our generated sub-claims
43: are of high quality and faithful to the ground truth.
44: Furthermore, the average number of words in the
45: generated sub-claims is 14 words, and they are
46: typically just one sentence long. This is aligned
47: with the intent behind the metric—to capture short
48: factual claims made by the original answer.
49: NLI model accurately predicts the entailment
50: of sub-claims. We further analyze our sub-claim
51: evaluation metrics by checking the error rate of
52: the final prediction of the NLI model. To this end,
53: we first manually annotate the entailment scores
54: between 40 outputs and their sub-claims (in total
55: of 120 pairs; these are the same questions from the
56: previous analysis). We then use the NLI model
57: to obtain the entailment scores for the output and
58: sub-claims. Using the human annotations as the
59: ground truth label, we found that the NLI model
60: achieved an accuracy of 80.0%.
61: B Dataset Statistics
62: For ASQA, human answers have an average length
63: of 65 words. For QAMPARI, each question has
64: on average 13 answers. For ELI5, human answers
65: have an average length of 131 words.

70: SNLI (Bowman et al., 2015), MNLI (Williams
71: et al., 2018), Fever (Thorne et al., 2018), Sci-
72: tail (Khot et al., 2018), PAWS (Zhang et al., 2019),
73: and VitaminC (Schuster et al., 2021). This model
74: uses the following prompt: “premise: {PREMISE}
75: hypothesis: {}” and outputs “1” if the premise
76: entails the hypothesis. We format each passage
77: (when used as premise) by the format of “Title:
78: {TITLE}\n{TEXT}” and concatenate all passages
79: with “\n” as a separator.

81: the question and the model output (or human an-
82: swer) by space. We truncate both the references
83: and the model generations to 100 words, as we
84: found MAUVE results are unstable beyond this
85: length for ELI5 (this is due to that ELI5 has a lot
86: of extremely long human answers).
87: Exact match for ASQA and QAMPARI. Both
88: ASQA and QAMPARI provide aliases for their
89: short answers. We normalize the response and the
90: short answers similarly to Rajpurkar et al. (2016)
91: and report the score with the best-matching aliases.
92: For ASQA, Stelmakh et al. (2022) also propose a
93: QA-based evaluation which we found to be not as
94: stable, and thus we do not report it in our paper.
